subject: Follow-up on additional sampling occasions at low-detection/abundance sites

messages.author: 985e455b8390aae3
messages.subject: Follow-up on additional sampling occasions at low-detection/abundance sites
parts:
Andy, I hope you don't mind if I chase this down a bit...

I think I may have given you a mistaken impression of our sampling scheme and used 'observation' ambiguously.

All sampling "occasions" (Js, in your RxJ matrix) were conducted similarly, and during each "J" the majority of counts ("y"s) were only 0-3 snakes.  So, our desired sample of 100 snakes per site (R) dictated only how many Js we conducted at each R.  The way I see it, each occasion (J) yielded a count (y) that was drawn as a Poisson process from a site (R) with a true but unknown N (abundance).  My assumption is that the more Js we have for any R, the more "defined" the latent distribution, conditioned on N, becomes.  Hence, equality of number of sampling occasions (Js) should not be important...just that those sites with more sampling occasions should contain more information in the likelihood.

I believe I've heard the advice before that optimal study design would dedicate more effort (more Js) toward areas with lower abundance and/or detectability, and in a sense that is what happened by our continuing to collect 'y's of 0-3 per J, sometimes 3 or 4, until we've repeated enough Js for a sum of 100 per R, with each J being nearly identical in its level of effort.

I agree that if, on any given occasion (J) we called it a night when some number of snakes were captured, that would be a totally different beast, but in our case, each occasion was standardized and every snake found was collected, with no stopping rule other than the time limit on our search protocols.

With this clarification, do you still think pcount or multinomPois are inappropriate with the unbalanced sampling occasions due to lower counts at some sites?  

Thanks,
Shane



   


On Tue, Nov 5, 2013 at 6:14 PM, Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
hi Shane,
 if you sampled until 100 snakes were obtained then the likelihood for any model in unmarked is wrong.  The likelihood would have to be formulated conditional on n=100 which, in general, will depend on the encounter probability parameters of the model and the true local population size.
 I don't see an obvious easy fix to this from where you're at. 
 Now , that said, I don't understand the variability in your observed sample sizes. So you sampled until n=100 or until some number of samples were made?

 In general the removal model should be appropriate for this type of removal data no matter how big the sample sizes are. However I think the stopping rule for sampling is important here.

regards
andy



On Tue, Nov 5, 2013 at 7:22 PM, Shane Siers <shane...@gmail.com> wrote:
Scenario:  Repeated surveys at 18 sites until desired samples of 100 snakes at each site were obtained.  Due to heterogeneity in capture rates (abundance?) numbers of observations per site range from 30 to 177 (see variability of counts per observation in chart below).  So, we have a VERY unbalanced sample effort wrt number of observations, but a balanced sample wrt total sum of counts at each site.

During preliminary model exploration, I used pcount with no problem and got reasonable results.  However, as snakes were removed, I thought it more appropriate to use multinomPois, type="removal".  Model runs were much more problematic, many problems with "Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se,...", "NaN"s in betas & ses, and ridiculous abundance estimates:

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Follow-up on additional sampling occasions at low-detection/abundance sites
parts:
Hey Shane, I think your approach seems valid.  I tried to simulate some data that mimics your own but its been tricky and the estimation using multinomPois has not gone smoothly (even with equal surveys across sites).  It sounds like your capture probabilities are extremely low which makes estimation using MLE very difficult, if not impossible, especially with only 18 sites.  The following code might be helpful to use for understanding your own data:

library(unmarked)
# Number of sites (R) and surveys (J)
R <- 100
J <- 200
# detection prob, E(N), simulated N
p <- 0.002
lambda <- 500
N <- rpois(R, rnorm(R,lambda,lambda*.1))

# multinomial detection probability
cp <- rep(p,J)
for (i in 2:length(cp)){
  cp[i] <- (1-p)^(i-1)*p}

# observation matrix
y <- matrix(NA, R, J)
for(i in 1:R) {
  y[i,] <- rmultinom(1, N[i], c(cp, 1-sum(cp)))[1:J]}

# total individuals removed
apply(y,1,sum)
# number of surveys to remove 100 individuals
indv100 <- apply(t(apply(y,1,cumsum)),1,FUN=function(x){min(which(x>100))})

# Cap the surveys when 100 individuals are removed
for (i in 1:nrow(y)){
  y[i,indv100:J]<-NA}

# Fit model
umf <- unmarkedFrameMPois(y=y, type="removal")
(fm <- multinomPois(~1 ~1, umf))

parts:
Dan, thanks for following up on this and taking the extra effort to provide an example.  I've latched onto your rationale that the low capture probabilities (lots of zeroes) make estimation with the multinomPois likelihood very problematic, especially with a multinomial term being calculated for each observation period, of which I have as many as 177 at one site.  I did try to subset my data to only use the first 30 occasions, so all sites got even sample effort (no NA's in the J's), but I still got nonsensical abundance estimates and NaN warnings.  On the other hand, pcount seems to be handling the full data set flawlessly and returns plausible estimates; with such high snake densities and low detection probabilities I think I can make a case that any effect of removal (average of 8 snakes per month) is negligible. That's the direction I'm pursuing at the moment...feel free to warn me off if you disagree.

Thanks again,
Shane
